days.guide: Give two new short folktales and the cold-read quiz without help; score with the rubric.

questions.a: State each theme, then explain how they are alike and different with evidence.

weeks.assessment_key: Comparison paragraphs: 4 = shared theme identified, details from both myths, differences explained; 3 = mostly; 2 = summaries; 1 = incomplete. Cold-read rubric (choose an unfamiliar grade-5 story from CommonLit): 4 = states a precise theme/central idea, explains character with 2+ exact quotations correctly punctuated and explained; 3 = accurate answer with at least one relevant quotation and explanation; 2 = accurate but general answer, evidence paraphrased or loosely connected; 1 = inaccurate or no evidence.

weeks.prep: Myth planning sheet; art supplies.
misconceptions: Forgetting to explain the phenomenon.
Rushing the key scene.
Weak verbs (went, got).

days.guide: Brainstorm phenomena together. Your child fills the planning sheet: characters, setting, conflict, and the explanation at the end.

questions.a: A natural phenomenon or custom.

days.guide: Your child drafts the myth with at least 4 lines of dialogue and a god, hero or trickster. Check dialogue punctuation.

questions.q: Punctuate: you will pay said Zeus
questions.a: “You will pay,” said Zeus.

days.guide: Your child highlights the travel or less important parts to summarize and the key scene to stretch. Replace 5 weak verbs with vivid ones.

questions.q: Replace 'went': The hero went up the mountain.
questions.a: The hero scrambled/climbed up the mountain.

days.guide: Your child types the final copy and illustrates key scenes, assembling a small book with a cover.

questions.a: They match key scenes.

days.guide: Your child reads the myth to an audience. Then give the cumulative roots quiz.

questions.a: Far; carry.

weeks.assessment_key: Myth rubric: 4 = explains a phenomenon, god/hero/trickster, dialogue, paced key scene, vivid verbs; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = little explanation; 1 = incomplete. Roots quiz key: spect see, port carry, struct build, rupt break, graph write, tele far, geo earth, chron time; prefixes un-, re-, dis-, mis-, pre-.

weeks.prep: Bookmark nps.gov park pages; library books; note-taking template.
misconceptions: Trusting any website. Check author, date, purpose.
Copying sentences. Paraphrase.
A synthesis that lists sources separately.

days.guide: Look at nps.gov pages together. Your child picks a park and writes 5 inquiry questions starting with how or why.

questions.a: How did glaciers shape Yosemite Valley?

days.guide: Show keyword searching (e.g., 'Yosemite glaciers formation'). Your child rates 4 websites on author, date, purpose and accuracy, then finds answers on nps.gov.

questions.a: It's the official National Park Service site with expert, current information.

days.guide: Your child takes paraphrased notes from 3 sources, organizing them by question and labeling each source.

questions.a: Restating in your own words.

days.guide: Model blending two sources in one sentence ('Both the NPS and…'). Your child writes a paragraph combining at least 2 sources on one question.

questions.a: Combining information from several sources into one explanation.

days.guide: Conference on the notes and source list. Your child completes a credibility checklist for each source.

questions.a: Author/organization, date, purpose, accuracy, .gov/.edu.

weeks.assessment_key: Notes: organized by question, 3 sources, paraphrased. Synthesis paragraph: 4 = combines 2+ sources smoothly with credit; 3 = 2 sources separately; 2 = one source; 1 = copied.

weeks.prep: Computer with free slideshow tool; images with credits.
misconceptions: Too much text on slides.
Media that doesn't support a main idea.
Forgetting image credits.

days.guide: Your child sketches 8 boxes: title, 5 content slides, conclusion and sources, with notes for each.

questions.a: Title, 5 content, conclusion, sources.

days.guide: Your child writes short slide text (bullets, not paragraphs) and a full speaker script for each slide.

questions.a: A few key words or short bullets.

days.guide: Your child adds a map, captioned photos and one audio or video clip, crediting each source on the slide or sources page.

questions.a: To respect creators and show sources.

days.guide: Your child proofreads slides and script, then times a practice run to about 5 minutes, trimming as needed.

questions.a: Rehearse with a timer and trim.

days.guide: Your child gives a full rehearsal for a family member who gives feedback on clarity, pace and visuals; revise accordingly.

questions.a: Clarity, pace, visuals.

weeks.assessment_key: Checklist: 8 slides storyboarded; concise text; full script; map, captioned photos, one media element; sources credited; ~5 minutes; edited.

weeks.prep: Slideshow; writing portfolio folder; list of books read; fluency passage from week 1 level; end-of-year cold read and essay prompt.
misconceptions: Reading from slides.
Summaries with too many details.
Reflections that just say 'I liked it.'

days.guide: Your child presents to family and answers questions. Score with the presentation rubric.

questions.q: What makes a strong answer to an audience question?
questions.a: A direct answer with a fact from research.

days.guide: Watch a family member's or online presentation together. Your child writes the main points and supporting details in a short summary.

questions.a: Main idea + 2–3 supporting details.

days.guide: Spread out the portfolio. Your child chooses the best narrative, informative and opinion pieces and writes a reflection card for each.

questions.q: What goes on a reflection card?
questions.a: Why you chose it, what you learned, what you'd improve.

days.guide: Your child lists and rates books read this year and writes a letter to next year's self about reading goals. Do a 1-minute fluency read and compare with week 1.

questions.a: Compare this WPM with week 1.

days.guide: Give the end-of-year cold read and on-demand essay without help. Score with the rubrics and celebrate growth.

questions.q: What makes a strong evidence answer?
questions.a: Claim, exact quotation, explanation.

weeks.assessment_key: Presentation rubric: 4 = clear, organized, well-paced with media and sources, confident answers; 3 = minor issues; 2 = disorganized; 1 = incomplete. Portfolio: 3 pieces with reflections. End-of-year: Cold-read rubric (choose an unfamiliar grade-5 story from CommonLit): 4 = states a precise theme/central idea, explains character with 2+ exact quotations correctly punctuated and explained; 3 = accurate answer with at least one relevant quotation and explanation; 2 = accurate but general answer, evidence paraphrased or loosely connected; 1 = inaccurate or no evidence. Essay: 4-level rubric for claim, evidence, organization, conventions. Fluency: compare to week 1 WPM.

HSS.overview: Fifth-grade history covers U.S. history from First Peoples to 1850, with a 50-states strand. Read sources together, ask 'who made this and why?', and have your child cite evidence. Map work and timelines anchor each unit; Friday checks use the keys.

weeks.prep: Print blank outline maps of North America and the U.S., gather an atlas (or online map), colored pencils, and make Northeast state/capital flashcards.
misconceptions: Mixing up latitude and longitude. Latitude lines run east–west but measure north–south ('lat is flat'); longitude lines run pole to pole.
Reading the map scale as exact distance without measuring. Use a ruler or paper strip against the scale bar.
Thinking New York City is New York's capital. The capital is Albany.

days.guide: Point to each map part (title, compass rose, scale, legend) and ask what it tells us. Model finding a place at a latitude/longitude by tracing the two lines with two fingers until they meet, then your child finds 5 places.

questions.a: Los Angeles, California.

questions.q: What does a map legend do?
questions.a: Explains what the symbols and colors on the map mean.

days.guide: Name each landform as you trace it on the atlas, then your child labels the outline map. Ask how each landform might help or block travel.

questions.q: Which mountains are older and lower, the Rockies or the Appalachians?
questions.a: The Appalachians, in the East; the Rockies in the West are higher and more rugged.

questions.q: Into what body of water does the Mississippi River flow?
questions.a: The Gulf of Mexico.

days.guide: Your child shades desert, forest, grassland and tundra regions using the atlas and writes one sentence per region about how people might live there (housing, food, clothing). Ask 'How do you know?' and have your child point to the source or map for each answer.

questions.q: How might living in the desert Southwest differ from living in the Eastern forests?
questions.a: Desert peoples must conserve water and build with clay and stone; forest peoples have wood for homes and abundant game and plants.

days.guide: Introduce the 11 Northeast states on a blank map, saying each state and capital aloud. Play flashcards in short rounds, keeping missed cards in a 'practice' pile.

questions.q: What is the capital of Pennsylvania? Of Vermont?
questions.a: Harrisburg; Montpelier.

days.guide: Give the map quiz without the atlas. Review any missed items by having your child find them again on the atlas.

questions.q: Name the large flat region between the Mississippi River and the Rocky Mountains.
questions.a: The Great Plains.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: landforms correctly labeled (Rockies, Appalachians, Great Plains, Mississippi River, Great Lakes, Atlantic and Pacific coasts); latitude/longitude items located within a few degrees; Northeast capitals: Maine–Augusta, New Hampshire–Concord, Vermont–Montpelier, Massachusetts–Boston, Rhode Island–Providence, Connecticut–Hartford, New York–Albany, New Jersey–Trenton, Pennsylvania–Harrisburg, Delaware–Dover, Maryland–Annapolis.

weeks.prep: Bookmark NPS photos of Mesa Verde and Taos Pueblo and images of Tlingit or Kwakwaka'wakw totem poles. Make salt dough (2 cups flour, 1 cup salt, ~3/4 cup water).
misconceptions: Thinking all Native peoples lived in tipis. Housing depended on the environment: adobe, cedar plank houses, longhouses, tipis.
Speaking of Native peoples only in the past tense. The Pueblo, Tlingit and Kwakwaka'wakw nations exist today.
Thinking totem poles are worshipped idols. They tell family histories, honor ancestors and record events.

days.guide: Look at the Mesa Verde photos together and ask: what materials did they build with? Where did water come from? Your child lists at least 5 ways the Ancestral Puebloans used land, water and stone.

questions.q: Why build homes in cliff alcoves?
questions.a: For protection from weather and enemies; stone overhangs gave shade in summer and shelter in winter.

days.guide: Read about the 'Three Sisters' (corn, beans, squash) and adobe building. Your child shapes a multi-story adobe dwelling with ladders and explains its features.

questions.q: Why were adobe homes good for the desert?
questions.a: Thick clay-brick walls keep the inside cool by day and warm at night; materials (clay, straw) were local.

days.guide: Read about salmon and cedar in the Pacific Northwest. Analyze a totem pole photo: what figures do you see, who made it, what might it tell?

questions.q: Why were salmon and cedar so important?
questions.a: Salmon was the main food, plentiful in rivers; cedar was used for plank houses, canoes, clothing and totem poles.

days.guide: Your child completes a chart comparing shelter, food, economy, government and customs for the Southwest and Pacific Northwest. Before finishing, have your child explain their work aloud in 2–3 sentences; correct any errors then.

questions.a: Pueblo peoples farmed corn in a dry land; Northwest peoples relied on abundant fish and trade and held potlatches to share wealth.

days.guide: Your child writes a paragraph explaining how environment shaped daily life in one region, using 3 details from the week. Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

questions.a: A ceremonial feast in the Pacific Northwest where hosts gave gifts to show status and mark important events.

weeks.assessment_key: Chart: 5 categories filled accurately for both regions. Paragraph rubric: 4 = clear topic sentence, three or more accurate, specific details or quotations from sources, explanation of how they support the point, conclusion; 3 = accurate with two details; 2 = general or partly inaccurate; 1 = off topic or incomplete.

weeks.prep: Find an excerpt of the Great Law of Peace and an image of the Hiawatha Belt (NMAI Native Knowledge 360). Choose a traditional Haudenosaunee or Lakota story from a reliable source.
misconceptions: Thinking Native nations had no organized government. The Haudenosaunee Confederacy had a written-in-wampum constitution and councils.
Thinking Plains peoples always lived on horseback. Horses arrived with the Spanish; they transformed Plains life after the 1600s.
Mixing up a longhouse and a tipi.

days.guide: Read about the Lakota and the bison. Your child draws a bison and labels uses for each part (meat, hide, bones, sinew, horns).

questions.a: Meat for food, hides for tipis and clothing, bones for tools, sinew for thread and bowstrings, horns for cups and spoons.

days.guide: Read about Haudenosaunee and Cherokee life. Your child makes a Venn diagram comparing a longhouse and a tipi.

questions.q: How is a longhouse different from a tipi?
questions.a: A longhouse is a long, permanent bark-covered home for several related families in a farming village; a tipi is a portable cone of poles and hides for moving with the bison.

days.guide: Read the excerpt and look at the Hiawatha Belt. Explain that the five nations (Mohawk, Oneida, Onondaga, Cayuga, Seneca) united under the Great Law, later joined by the Tuscarora.

questions.q: What does the Hiawatha Belt show?
questions.a: Five symbols linked by a line — the five nations joined in peace, with the Onondaga (Great Tree of Peace) at the center.
A Grand Council of chiefs from each nation, chosen by clan mothers, made decisions by discussion and agreement.

days.guide: Read a traditional story aloud. Your child identifies what it teaches about values or nature.

questions.q: What do many traditional stories teach?
questions.a: Respect for nature, living in balance, and values like generosity and courage.

days.guide: Give the quiz. Your child explains one feature of Haudenosaunee government in writing.

questions.q: What role did clan mothers play?
questions.a: They chose and could remove the chiefs who sat on the council.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key (suggested): 1) Plains peoples relied on the bison 2) tipis were portable 3) longhouses housed several families 4) Haudenosaunee = Five (later Six) Nations 5) Great Law of Peace united them 6) clan mothers chose chiefs 7) Cherokee were Eastern Woodlands farmers. Primary-source sheet: describes belt symbols and explains unity.

weeks.prep: Poster board, art supplies, and research sources from NMAI Native Knowledge 360 or a nation's official website. Southeast flashcards.
misconceptions: Copying facts without connecting them to geography.
Thinking Native nations ended long ago. Many have governments, languages and cultural programs today.
Mixing up Southeast capitals.

days.guide: Help your child pick a nation and find 2–3 reliable sources (NMAI Native Knowledge 360, the nation's own website, a library book). They take notes in five labeled boxes: homeland, food, shelter, government, stories.

questions.a: Northeastern Arizona, on mesas.

days.guide: Help your child find the nation's official website. They record one fact about its present-day government or culture.

questions.q: Name a present-day Native nation government.
questions.a: The Cherokee Nation (Tahlequah, Oklahoma) has an elected Principal Chief and council.

days.guide: Your child creates a poster or museum card set showing how geography shaped the nation's life, with pictures and captions. Ask 'How do you know?' and have your child point to the source or map for each answer.

questions.a: How the environment shaped that part of life.

days.guide: Say each Southeast state and capital aloud while pointing to the map, then quiz with flashcards. Your child shades the Cherokee, Creek (Muscogee) and Seminole homelands and labels them.

questions.a: Florida.
Nashville.

days.guide: Your child presents the poster in 2–3 minutes while you ask one follow-up question. Then give the Unit 1 test without notes.

questions.q: Name one region and its main shelter.
questions.a: Southwest–adobe pueblos; Pacific Northwest–cedar plank houses; Plains–tipis; Eastern Woodlands–longhouses.

weeks.assessment_key: Project rubric: 4 = accurate homeland, food, shelter, government, stories, clear geography connection, present-day fact, neat; 3 = minor gaps; 2 = missing categories; 1 = incomplete. Unit 1 test: regions matched to peoples and shelters; Great Law of Peace; Southeast capitals: Virginia–Richmond, West Virginia–Charleston, Kentucky–Frankfort, Tennessee–Nashville, North Carolina–Raleigh, South Carolina–Columbia, Georgia–Atlanta, Florida–Tallahassee, Alabama–Montgomery, Mississippi–Jackson.

weeks.prep: Images of an astrolabe and caravel; cardboard, string, washer, protractor and straw for an astrolabe.
misconceptions: Thinking explorers went only for adventure. Main motives were trade, wealth, religion and national competition.
Thinking people then believed the Earth was flat. Educated Europeans knew it was round; the question was its size.
Thinking an astrolabe finds longitude. It measures latitude by angle of the sun or a star.

days.guide: Read about motives: trade routes to Asia's spices, gold, spreading Christianity, the Reconquista's end in 1492, and rivalry among nations. Your child ranks them with evidence.

questions.q: Why did Europeans want a sea route to Asia?
questions.a: Overland trade routes were long and controlled by others; a sea route would bring spices and silk more cheaply.

days.guide: Build an astrolabe: tape a straw to the protractor's straight edge, hang a weighted string from the center. Sight the top of a tall object and read the angle.

questions.q: What did sailors measure with an astrolabe?
questions.a: The angle of the sun or North Star above the horizon, to find latitude.

days.guide: Compare pictures of a caravel and older ships. Your child explains features that helped long voyages.

questions.a: Triangular (lateen) sails let it sail into the wind; it was small, fast and could explore shallow coasts.

days.guide: Explain that voyages cost a fortune and sponsors wanted a return. Your child writes and delivers a 1-minute pitch naming the goal, route, and what the sponsor gains.

questions.a: King Ferdinand and Queen Isabella of Spain.

days.guide: Give the quiz without notes, then have your child correct missed items using the week's readings. Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

questions.q: What does 'God, gold and glory' mean?
questions.a: Spreading Christianity, gaining wealth and winning fame for the nation.

weeks.assessment_key: Quiz key: 1) motives: trade, wealth, religion, competition 2) astrolabe measures latitude 3) compass shows direction 4) caravel lateen sails 5) sponsors were monarchs/merchants. Pitch rubric: states goal, benefits to sponsor, plan, persuasive tone.

weeks.prep: Columbus's October 12, 1492 journal excerpt (National Archives or Library of Congress education pages) and a map of Coronado's and de Soto's routes. Preview materials on forced labor and disease.
misconceptions: Thinking Columbus 'discovered' an empty land. Millions of people already lived in the Americas.
Thinking the Columbian Exchange was only goods. It included diseases that devastated Native populations.
Confusing Coronado (Southwest) and de Soto (Southeast).

days.guide: Read the journal excerpt aloud. Your child lists what Columbus observed and what he wanted.

questions.a: Gold, land for Spain, and to convert people to Christianity; he wrote the Taíno would make good servants.

days.guide: Read about Taíno society and the impact of contact. Your child compares to Columbus's account in a T-chart.

questions.q: What happened to the Taíno population?
questions.a: It fell drastically due to disease, violence and forced labor.

days.guide: Trace Coronado's (1540–42) and de Soto's (1539–42) routes. Your child records goals, obstacles and results.

questions.a: The legendary Seven Cities of Gold (Cíbola); he found none.
The Mississippi River; he died on the expedition.

days.guide: Your child sorts items that crossed the Atlantic each way and explains one lasting effect. Before finishing, have your child explain their work aloud in 2–3 sentences; correct any errors then.

questions.q: Name items from the Americas to Europe and from Europe to the Americas.
questions.a: Americas → Europe: corn, potatoes, tomatoes, cacao. Europe → Americas: horses, cattle, wheat, smallpox.

days.guide: Your child writes a paragraph evaluating Columbus's legacy from two perspectives with evidence. Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

questions.q: Why do people disagree about Columbus?
questions.a: He began lasting contact between continents, but his actions led to suffering for Native peoples.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = clear topic sentence, three or more accurate, specific details or quotations from sources, explanation of how they support the point, conclusion; 3 = accurate with two details; 2 = general or partly inaccurate; 1 = off topic or incomplete. Route map: Coronado (Southwest to Kansas) and de Soto (Southeast across the Mississippi) correctly traced.

weeks.prep: Outline map of North America, explorer cards (Cabot, Cartier, Champlain, Hudson, Columbus, Coronado).
misconceptions: Thinking the Northwest Passage existed as hoped. No practical route through North America was found.
Confusing Hudson's sponsors. He sailed for the Dutch (1609) and the English (1610).
Coloring claims as if borders were firm.

days.guide: Read short bios of Cabot (England, 1497) and Cartier (France, 1534–36). Your child traces both routes on the outline map in different colors and notes each sponsor and finding.

questions.q: What did Cabot's voyage give England?
questions.a: A claim to North America.

days.guide: Read about Champlain (founded Quebec, 1608) and Hudson (Dutch voyage 1609, English voyage 1610). Ask why so many explorers looked for a Northwest Passage and whether they found one.

questions.a: A hoped-for water route through North America to Asia.

days.guide: Your child fills a matrix (sponsor, goal, obstacles, accomplishments) for Columbus, Coronado, Cabot, Cartier, Champlain and Hudson. Check each row against the readings.

questions.a: Samuel de Champlain, 1608.

days.guide: Use an atlas showing about 1650 claims. Your child colors each nation's claim with a key and labels one settlement for each.

questions.q: Which country claimed most of South America's east coast?
questions.a: Portugal (Brazil).

days.guide: Give the map quiz without the atlas; review any missed route by retracing it. Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

questions.a: The St. Lawrence River.

weeks.assessment_key: Matrix: sponsor, goal, obstacles, accomplishments for 6 explorers. Map quiz key: Spain–Southwest, Florida, Mexico; France–St. Lawrence and Mississippi; England–Atlantic coast; Netherlands–Hudson River; Russia–Alaska; Sweden–Delaware River; Portugal–Brazil.

weeks.prep: Map of Atlantic trade routes; an age-appropriate excerpt from Olaudah Equiano's narrative (1789). Preview it — it describes the Middle Passage. Midwest flashcards.
misconceptions: Thinking the 'triangle' was a single fixed route. Many routes and goods.
Thinking enslaved Africans came willingly.
Mixing up Midwest capitals.

days.guide: Draw a triangle connecting Europe, West Africa and the Americas on a map. Your child labels the goods on each leg and the direction of travel.

questions.q: What goods went on each leg?
questions.a: Europe → Africa: cloth, guns, rum; Africa → Americas: enslaved people; Americas → Europe: sugar, tobacco, cotton.

days.guide: Read the excerpt aloud together and pause to discuss feelings and facts. Ask what Equiano's account shows that a trade map cannot.

questions.a: Crowded, filthy holds, sickness, chains and terror.

days.guide: Introduce the 12 Midwest states and capitals on the blank map, then drill with flashcards. Your child labels the map from memory at the end.

questions.a: Jefferson City; Pierre.

days.guide: Your child places 6–8 explorations from 1492 to 1610 on a timeline in order. Review vocabulary words (sponsor, colony, Northwest Passage, Columbian Exchange) with quick definitions.

questions.q: Put in order: Cartier, Columbus, Champlain.
questions.a: Columbus (1492), Cartier (1534), Champlain (1608).

days.guide: Give the Unit 2 test independently and review mistakes using the timeline and maps. Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

questions.q: Which country did Hudson sail for in 1609?
questions.a: The Netherlands.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 2 test key: exploration motives; astrolabe; Columbus and the Taíno; Coronado, de Soto; Cabot, Cartier, Champlain, Hudson; Columbian Exchange; Atlantic trade; Midwest capitals: Ohio–Columbus, Indiana–Indianapolis, Illinois–Springfield, Michigan–Lansing, Wisconsin–Madison, Minnesota–Saint Paul, Iowa–Des Moines, Missouri–Jefferson City, North Dakota–Bismarck, South Dakota–Pierre, Nebraska–Lincoln, Kansas–Topeka.

weeks.prep: John Smith's 1612 map of Virginia (Library of Congress); photos of Jamestown.
misconceptions: Believing the Pocahontas 'rescue' story is proven. It comes only from John Smith's later account.
Thinking Jamestown succeeded quickly.
Thinking Pocahontas was an adult in 1607. She was about 11.

days.guide: Read about the Virginia Company (an investment company hoping for gold and profit) and the 1607 landing. Your child lists at least 5 problems the settlers faced.

questions.a: Swampy land, disease, bad water, hunger (the 'Starving Time' 1609–10), conflict with the Powhatan.

days.guide: Look at Smith's 1612 map together; note that it is oriented with west at the top. Your child circles Powhatan towns and writes what the map shows about who already lived there.

questions.a: Many Powhatan towns along rivers — the land was already populated.

days.guide: Read about the Powhatan Confederacy and Pocahontas. Your child sorts statements into 'documented fact' and 'legend' (e.g., her marriage to John Rolfe is fact; the rescue story comes only from Smith's later writing).

questions.a: She was Powhatan's daughter, was captured by the English, married John Rolfe in 1614 and died in England in 1617.

days.guide: Explain how John Rolfe's sweet tobacco (about 1612) became a cash crop and how the Anglican Church was the official church. Ask: what new problems did tobacco create?

questions.a: Rolfe's tobacco became a profitable cash crop.

days.guide: Your child makes a cause-and-effect chart with 4+ rows from Jamestown's struggles and successes. Check each effect truly follows its cause.

questions.a: Profit, need for more land and labor, conflict with the Powhatan.

weeks.assessment_key: Map analysis: notes towns, rivers, purpose. Cause-effect chart: 4+ accurate pairs.

weeks.prep: Text of the Mayflower Compact; excerpt of William Bradford's Of Plymouth Plantation.
misconceptions: Thinking the 1621 harvest was the first 'Thanksgiving' as celebrated today.
Thinking Pilgrims and Puritans were identical.
Thinking Squanto learned English from the Pilgrims.

days.guide: Read about the 1620 voyage and the Wampanoag. Your child notes who Massasoit and Tisquantum were and how they shaped the colony's survival.

questions.a: He had been kidnapped and taken to Europe years earlier.

days.guide: Read the Compact aloud (it is one sentence). Your child paraphrases it in plain words and explains how it is an early example of self-government.

questions.a: Colonists agreed to make and obey fair laws for the common good — an early example of self-government.

days.guide: Read Bradford's excerpt on the first winter and the 1621 harvest. Then read a Wampanoag perspective (e.g., from Plimoth Patuxet's resources) and compare.

questions.a: About half the Pilgrims died.

days.guide: Read about John Winthrop and the 1630 Massachusetts Bay Colony. Your child lists 3–4 Puritan values (hard work, education to read the Bible, strict community rules).

questions.q: What did 'city upon a hill' mean?
questions.a: Their community should be a model for the world.

days.guide: Give the quiz, then your child writes a 2-sentence summary of the Compact. Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

questions.q: When was the Mayflower Compact signed?

weeks.assessment_key: Paraphrase: captures agreement to form a government and obey just laws. Quiz key: 1620, Plymouth, Wampanoag, Massasoit, Squanto, Bradford, Winthrop, Massachusetts Bay 1630.

weeks.prep: Map of New England colonies, colonial economy cards.
misconceptions: Thinking Puritans believed in religious freedom for everyone.
Thinking New England was mainly farming.
Confusing Hooker and Hutchinson.

days.guide: Read about Roger Williams. Ask: Why would leaders banish someone for his ideas? Your child records his beliefs and how Rhode Island was different.

questions.a: He argued for separation of church and government and fair dealings with Native peoples.

days.guide: Read short bios of Anne Hutchinson and Thomas Hooker. Your child makes a Venn diagram of their disagreements with Puritan leaders and what each did next.

questions.a: Hartford, Connecticut (1636).

days.guide: Your child shades rocky soil, forests and harbors on a New England map. Then they explain in writing how these led to fishing, shipbuilding and trade.

questions.a: Rocky soil, forests, good harbors.

days.guide: Brainstorm details first (school with a hornbook, chores, Sunday meeting). Your child writes a diary entry with at least 5 accurate details.

questions.a: Attending a long Sunday meeting.

days.guide: Your child labels the New England colonies, then takes the quiz on founders and reasons. Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

questions.q: Name the four New England colonies.
questions.a: Massachusetts, Rhode Island, Connecticut, New Hampshire.

weeks.assessment_key: Diary rubric: 5 accurate details. Map quiz key: MA, RI, CT, NH.

weeks.prep: Excerpt of William Penn's letter to the Lenape (1681); map of the 13 colonies.
misconceptions: Thinking Middle Colonies were all Quaker.
Thinking Georgia was founded early.
Mixing up regions.

days.guide: Read about William Penn, the Quakers and his 'holy experiment.' Read his letter to the Lenape; your child lists what he promised.

questions.q: What did Penn promise the Lenape?
questions.a: To live in peace and deal fairly.

days.guide: Explain that the Dutch colony of New Netherland was taken by England in 1664 and renamed New York. Ask why fertile land and a mild climate made the Middle Colonies 'breadbasket' colonies.
Read about Lord Baltimore (Maryland, 1634), the Carolinas and Georgia (1732). Your child notes the reason each was founded.

questions.a: James Oglethorpe in 1732, for debtors and as a buffer against Spanish Florida.

days.guide: Your child fills a chart comparing New England, Middle and Southern colonies on geography, economy, religion and founders. Before finishing, have your child explain their work aloud in 2–3 sentences; correct any errors then.

questions.a: Grew lots of wheat.

days.guide: Your child labels all 13 colonies on a blank map, then takes the quiz. Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

questions.a: Maryland, Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia.

weeks.assessment_key: 13 colonies map: all labeled. Regions chart: geography, economy, religion, founders accurate.

weeks.prep: Excerpt from Benjamin Franklin's Autobiography on Whitefield; materials for a craft (cream and jar for butter). South Central flashcards. Write the Unit 3 test.
misconceptions: Thinking the Great Awakening was a single event.
Thinking apprentices were paid workers.
Mixing up South Central capitals.

days.guide: Read about Jonathan Edwards and George Whitefield, then Franklin's account. Discuss how emotional preaching encouraged people to think for themselves about religion and authority.

questions.q: What did Franklin do when he heard Whitefield?
questions.a: He emptied his pockets into the collection plate despite planning not to.

days.guide: Read about apprentices (young people who learned a trade from a master for several years) and artisans. Your child chooses one trade and researches its tools and products.

questions.a: Barrels.

days.guide: Choose one activity with adult help (shaking cream in a jar for butter is easiest). Afterward, your child writes how long it took and what it shows about colonial work.

questions.a: Shaking cream makes fat clump.

days.guide: Review Southeast states with flashcards, then add Texas, Oklahoma, Arkansas and Louisiana. Your child labels all on a blank map.

questions.a: Baton Rouge.

days.guide: Give the Unit 3 test independently; review errors with the 13 colonies map. Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

questions.a: William Penn.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 3 test key: Jamestown 1607; tobacco; Plymouth 1620; Mayflower Compact; Massachusetts Bay; Roger Williams; Penn; Oglethorpe; Great Awakening. South Central capitals: Texas–Austin, Oklahoma–Oklahoma City, Arkansas–Little Rock, Louisiana–Baton Rouge.

weeks.prep: Comparison chart; trade goods list.
misconceptions: Thinking colonists could trade freely.
Thinking Spanish missions were only churches.
Thinking France had many settlers.

days.guide: Play a simple trade: your child (colonist) sells raw cotton cheaply to you (England), then must buy back a shirt at a high price. Discuss who benefits and why colonists might resent it.

questions.a: England.

days.guide: Read how colonists ran farms, shops and ships for profit. Your child explains in their own words what free enterprise means.

questions.a: People own businesses and make choices for profit.

days.guide: Read about Spanish missions and presidios (including California) and French fur-trading posts. Your child notes the purpose of each.

questions.a: Spread Christianity and control land.

days.guide: Your child fills a chart comparing British, Spanish and French colonies on government, economy, religion and relations with Native peoples. Before finishing, have your child explain their work aloud in 2–3 sentences; correct any errors then.

questions.q: How did French relate to Natives?
questions.a: Mostly trade partnerships.

days.guide: Your child writes a paragraph explaining one major difference between British and Spanish colonies with two details. Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

questions.a: British colonies had more self-government.

weeks.assessment_key: Chart and Paragraph rubric: 4 = clear topic sentence, three or more accurate, specific details or quotations from sources, explanation of how they support the point, conclusion; 3 = accurate with two details; 2 = general or partly inaccurate; 1 = off topic or incomplete.

weeks.prep: Phillis Wheatley poem 'On Being Brought from Africa to America' (1773), 1688 Germantown Petition excerpt, Equiano excerpt. Preview for sensitive content.
misconceptions: Thinking slavery existed only in the South.
Thinking enslaved people did not resist.
Thinking slavery was legal from 1619.

days.guide: Read about the 1619 arrival of enslaved Africans at Point Comfort, Virginia. Explain how laws over the next decades made slavery lifelong and inherited.

questions.a: Children of enslaved mothers were enslaved.

days.guide: Read about enslaved families' work, culture, music and faith. Ask how they kept traditions alive despite cruelty.

questions.a: Music, stories, faith, family.

days.guide: Read about forms of resistance (slowdowns, breaking tools, escape, the 1739 Stono Rebellion). Your child records examples in a chart.

questions.a: A 1739 uprising in South Carolina.

days.guide: Read the 1688 Germantown Petition and Wheatley's poem. Your child notes each author's argument or message.

questions.q: What did the Germantown Petition argue?
questions.a: Slavery is wrong; treat others as you would want to be treated.

days.guide: Your child writes a paragraph using two sources explaining how slavery became institutionalized in the South. Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

questions.a: Through laws making it lifelong and hereditary.

weeks.assessment_key: Paragraph rubric: 4 = clear topic sentence, three or more accurate, specific details or quotations from sources, explanation of how they support the point, conclusion; 3 = accurate with two details; 2 = general or partly inaccurate; 1 = off topic or incomplete.

weeks.prep: Description of the House of Burgesses; family meeting agenda. Write the Unit 4 test.
misconceptions: Thinking everyone could vote.
Thinking the Magna Carta was American.
Thinking town meetings were everywhere.

days.guide: Read about the Magna Carta (1215) and English Bill of Rights (1689). Your child lists 3 rights colonists expected as English subjects.

questions.a: Even the king must obey the law.

days.guide: Read about the House of Burgesses (1619). Your child notes who could vote and how it worked.
Choose a real household decision. Your child leads a family meeting with an agenda, majority vote and written minutes.

questions.a: More than half decides.

days.guide: Discuss who could not vote in colonial assemblies. Ask why limits existed and how that compares to today.

questions.a: Mostly white, male landowners.

days.guide: Give the Unit 4 test independently. Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

questions.q: What was the first representative assembly in English America?
questions.a: The House of Burgesses.

weeks.assessment_key: Minutes: date, attendees, motion, vote. Unit 4 test key: mercantilism, slavery laws, Stono, Magna Carta, House of Burgesses, voting limits.

weeks.prep: Image of Benjamin West's 'Penn's Treaty with the Indians' (1771); fur trade map.
misconceptions: Thinking paintings are photos.
Thinking only colonists gave technology.
Thinking cooperation lasted.

days.guide: Read about Native farming knowledge (corn, fish fertilizer, the Three Sisters). Your child lists resources colonists learned to use.

questions.a: Growing corn with fish fertilizer and the Three Sisters.

days.guide: Map French and Dutch fur trade networks. Your child lists what Native traders and Europeans each gained.

questions.a: Metal tools, cloth, guns.

days.guide: Look at West's 1771 painting of the 1682 treaty. Discuss how a painting made about 90 years later can idealize events.

questions.q: Why can a later painting shape memory?
questions.a: It shows an idealized version.

days.guide: Your child lists words (moccasin, raccoon, canoe), foods (corn, squash, turkey) and technologies (canoes, snowshoes) exchanged. Before finishing, have your child explain their work aloud in 2–3 sentences; correct any errors then.

questions.a: Moccasin, raccoon.

days.guide: Your child writes a summary of three forms of cooperation with examples. Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

questions.a: Farming knowledge, trade, alliances.

weeks.assessment_key: Painting analysis and summary rubric: accurate details, explanation.

weeks.prep: Excerpt of Mary Rowlandson's narrative or Metacom's grievances; timeline template. Preview violent content.
misconceptions: Thinking all Native nations were united.
Thinking wars were one-sided.
Confusing the wars.

days.guide: Read about the Powhatan Wars. Your child lists causes, especially expanding tobacco farms on Powhatan land.

questions.a: Colonists took land for tobacco.

days.guide: Read about the Pequot War (1636–38) and the 1637 Mystic massacre. Discuss how colonists and Native allies fought together.

questions.a: English and allied Narragansett and Mohegan warriors burned a Pequot fort, killing hundreds.

days.guide: Read Metacom's grievances (1675). Your child explains why he resisted colonial expansion.

questions.a: Colonists took land and imposed laws.

days.guide: Read about rivalries (Haudenosaunee vs. Huron). Discuss how Europeans used them to gain allies.

questions.a: Haudenosaunee vs. Huron over fur trade.

days.guide: Your child builds a timeline of the colonial wars with causes and effects, then takes the quiz. Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

questions.a: Powhatan Wars (1610s–40s), Pequot War (1636–38), King Philip's War (1675–76).

weeks.assessment_key: Timeline: causes and effects. Quiz key: dates, leaders, causes.

weeks.prep: Franklin's 'Join, or Die' cartoon (1754); maps of 1754 and 1763. West flashcards. Write the Unit 5 test.
misconceptions: Thinking the war was against Native peoples. It was Britain vs. France, each with Native allies.
Thinking colonists welcomed the Proclamation.
Thinking the war ended in 1754.

days.guide: Map British, French and Native claims to the Ohio Valley. Explain why the war began in 1754.

questions.a: Britain and France both claimed the Ohio Valley.

days.guide: Look at the cartoon together. Your child explains the snake segments and the message of unity.

questions.a: Colonies must unite or be destroyed.

days.guide: Chart Native nations' alliances. Compare 1754 and 1763 maps.

questions.a: Canada and land east of the Mississippi.

days.guide: Read about Pontiac's resistance and the Proclamation of 1763. Your child explains colonists' anger.

questions.a: It banned settlement west of the Appalachians.

days.guide: Give the Unit 5 test and review West states and capitals. Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

weeks.assessment_key: Cartoon analysis: segments as colonies, unity message. Unit 5 test key: cooperation, wars, French and Indian War, Proclamation. West capitals: Montana–Helena, Idaho–Boise, Wyoming–Cheyenne, Nevada–Carson City, Utah–Salt Lake City, Colorado–Denver, Arizona–Phoenix, New Mexico–Santa Fe, Washington–Olympia, Oregon–Salem, California–Sacramento, Alaska–Juneau, Hawaii–Honolulu.

weeks.prep: Image of a 1765 tax stamp; Stamp Act broadside (Library of Congress).
misconceptions: Thinking taxes were very high.
Thinking all colonists protested.
Confusing Stamp Act and Townshend Acts.

days.guide: Role-play Parliament and colonists. Your child argues both sides.

questions.a: The war protected colonists, so they should help pay.

days.guide: Examine the tax stamp and broadside. Your child lists taxed items.

questions.a: Newspapers, legal documents, playing cards.

days.guide: Read about the Stamp Act Congress, boycotts and the Sons and Daughters of Liberty. Ask 'How do you know?' and have your child point to the source or map for each answer.

questions.q: What did the Daughters of Liberty do?
questions.a: Made homespun cloth to boycott British goods.

days.guide: Explain the Townshend Acts. Your child calculates costs of taxed items.

questions.a: Glass, lead, paint, paper, tea.

days.guide: Your child writes a protest letter using 'no taxation without representation.' Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

questions.q: What does 'no taxation without representation' mean?
questions.a: Colonists had no elected members in Parliament.

weeks.assessment_key: Letter rubric: 4 = persuasive, accurate taxes, uses phrase; 3 = minor; 2 = weak; 1 = incomplete.

weeks.prep: Paul Revere's 1770 engraving; Captain Preston's account excerpt.
misconceptions: Thinking the engraving is accurate.
Thinking the Tea Party was spontaneous.
Mixing up Coercive Acts.

days.guide: Look closely at Revere's engraving. Your child lists details that make the British look guilty.

questions.a: Soldiers firing in line, an officer ordering them.

days.guide: Compare the engraving with Preston's account. Discuss why stories differ.

questions.a: Different perspectives and purposes.

days.guide: Read about the Tea Act and Tea Party. Your child writes Patriot and Loyalist headlines.

questions.a: Patriots defend liberty!

days.guide: List the Coercive Acts. Explain how Committees of Correspondence helped colonies unite.

questions.q: What did the Coercive Acts do?
questions.a: Closed Boston Harbor and limited Massachusetts self-government.

days.guide: Give the quiz; your child creates a cause-and-effect chain from 1765 to 1774. Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

questions.a: Stamp Act → protests → Townshend Acts → Boston Massacre → Tea Act → Tea Party → Coercive Acts.

weeks.assessment_key: Engraving analysis and chain: accurate order.

weeks.prep: Patrick Henry's speech excerpt (1775); map of Lexington and Concord.
misconceptions: Thinking independence was declared in 1775.
Thinking Revere rode alone.
Thinking all colonists were Patriots.

days.guide: Read about the First Continental Congress (1774). Your child lists decisions.

questions.a: Boycott British goods and meet again.

days.guide: Read Henry's speech excerpt; your child performs it with expression and explains its argument. Model the first item yourself, then let your child finish while you check accuracy against the source.

questions.a: Fight for freedom.

days.guide: Map Revere's and Dawes's rides and the battles (April 19, 1775). Ask 'How do you know?' and have your child point to the source or map for each answer.

questions.a: William Dawes (and Samuel Prescott).

days.guide: Explain how the Second Continental Congress created the army and chose Washington. Before finishing, have your child explain their work aloud in 2–3 sentences; correct any errors then.

questions.a: George Washington.

days.guide: Your child makes a Patriot vs. Loyalist T-chart, then takes the quiz.

questions.a: Stay loyal to the king.

weeks.assessment_key: Performance: expressive. T-chart: 3 beliefs each.

weeks.prep: Declaration transcript (National Archives); Common Sense excerpt. Write the Unit 6 test.
misconceptions: Thinking the Declaration created a government.
Thinking Jefferson wrote alone.
Thinking 'all men' included everyone then.

days.guide: Read a Common Sense excerpt. Your child explains how Paine persuaded ordinary people.

questions.a: Plain language and common sense.

days.guide: Learn about the Committee of Five and Jefferson's draft. Model the first item yourself, then let your child finish while you check accuracy against the source.

questions.a: Thomas Jefferson.

days.guide: Your child paraphrases the second paragraph and explains unalienable rights and consent of the governed. Ask 'How do you know?' and have your child point to the source or map for each answer.

questions.a: Life, liberty, pursuit of happiness.

days.guide: Your child matches 5 grievances to earlier events. Before finishing, have your child explain their work aloud in 2–3 sentences; correct any errors then.

questions.a: Taxes without consent → Stamp Act.

days.guide: Give the Unit 6 test. Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

weeks.assessment_key: Paraphrase: rights, consent. Unit 6 test key: taxes, Massacre, Tea Party, Coercive Acts, Continental Congresses, Lexington and Concord, Declaration.

weeks.prep: Revolutionary War battle map; Valley Forge letter excerpt.
misconceptions: Thinking Americans won every battle.
Thinking Valley Forge was a battle.
Thinking France joined immediately.

days.guide: Your child charts strengths and weaknesses of both armies. Pause after the reading to ask your child to retell the key facts in their own words before writing anything.

questions.a: Fighting on home ground.

days.guide: Map Bunker Hill, New York and Trenton. Model the first item yourself, then let your child finish while you check accuracy against the source.

questions.a: A surprise victory boosted morale.

days.guide: Read about Saratoga; your child explains why it brought France in. Ask 'How do you know?' and have your child point to the source or map for each answer.

questions.a: Convinced France to ally.

days.guide: Read Washington's letter; your child lists soldiers' needs. Before finishing, have your child explain their work aloud in 2–3 sentences; correct any errors then.

questions.a: Food, clothing, shoes.

days.guide: Your child creates an annotated battle map. Use the assessment key to score it, then reteach any missed idea with the week's sources.

questions.a: Lexington/Concord, Bunker Hill, Trenton, Saratoga, Yorktown.

weeks.assessment_key: Annotated map: 5 battles with significance.

weeks.prep: Biography cards; map of Spanish Gulf Coast campaigns.
misconceptions: Thinking Americans fought alone.
Thinking all Native nations sided with Britain.
Thinking Black Americans fought only for Patriots.

days.guide: Read about Franklin's negotiations and the 1778 alliance. Pause after the reading to ask your child to retell the key facts in their own words before writing anything.

questions.a: Troops, navy, money.

days.guide: Your child creates 4 biography cards. Model the first item yourself, then let your child finish while you check accuracy against the source.

questions.a: Captured British forts on the Gulf Coast.

days.guide: Read about the Oneida and Joseph Brant; your child explains each side's reasons. Ask 'How do you know?' and have your child point to the source or map for each answer.

questions.q: Why did Brant side with Britain?
questions.a: To protect Mohawk lands.

MATH.overview: Teach each day as model → guided practice → independent practice: show the strategy with a concrete model (disks, strips, cubes), do one or two together, then let your child work alone while you watch for the misconceptions listed each week. Ask for an estimate before every computation and a check after. Plan about 60 minutes a day; Fridays are quizzes or unit tests — grade them with the keys and reteach what was missed before moving on.

weeks.prep: Print or draw a place value chart from millions to thousandths; gather place value disks (or paper squares labeled 1,000,000 down to 0.001) and a whiteboard. Prepare a list of 10 numbers to dictate, e.g. 4,382,615.207.
misconceptions: Thinking the decimal point moves when multiplying by 10. Show on the chart that the digits shift one place left while the point stays put.
Reading 0.07 as 'seven tenths.' Have the child say the name of the place of the last digit: 7 hundredths.
Believing a longer decimal is larger. Compare values with disks: 0.4 (four tenths disks) beats 0.399.

days.guide: Draw the chart together, naming each place aloud from millions to thousandths. Dictate 10 numbers; the child writes each in the chart and names the value of the digit you underline. Check that zeros hold empty places.

questions.q: In 4,382,615.207, what is the value of the 8? Of the 7?
questions.a: 8 is in the ten-thousands place, so 80,000. 7 is in the thousandths place, so 7 thousandths (0.007).

questions.q: Write 'two million, fifty thousand, three and six hundredths' in standard form.

days.guide: Lay out 4 tenths disks, then show 10 groups of them: trade every 10 tenths for a one to get 4 ones, then repeat to get 40. The child records 8 'times 10' statements with arrows showing each digit moving one place left.

questions.q: What is 0.36 × 10? Explain with place value.
questions.a: 3.6 — the 3 tenths become 3 ones and the 6 hundredths become 6 tenths; each digit moves one place left.

days.guide: Model 300 ÷ 10 by trading each hundred disk for 10 tens and sharing into 10 groups (30 each); repeat for 30 and 3 (3 becomes 30 tenths, so 0.3 each). The child writes 8 '1/10 of' statements and draws digits shifting one place right.

questions.a: 0.07 (7 hundredths).

days.guide: Write 555.555 and have the child give the value of each 5 (500, 50, 5, 0.5, 0.05, 0.005). Ask how each compares to its neighbor: 10 times the one on its right, 1/10 the one on its left. Then work the 10 'how many times greater' problems.

questions.q: In 555.555, how many times greater is the 5 in the tens place than the 5 in the tenths place?
In 7,707, how does the value of the first 7 compare to the second 7?
questions.a: The first 7 is 7,000 and the second is 700, so it is 10 times greater.

days.guide: Give the 12-question quiz below without help, then have the child write one sentence explaining why the decimal point stays fixed. Correct together using disks or the chart.

questions.q: Why does the decimal point never move when you multiply by 10?
questions.a: The decimal point marks the boundary between ones and tenths; multiplying by 10 makes each digit worth 10 times as much, so the digits shift one place left past the fixed point.

weeks.assessment_key: Suggested quiz and key: 1) Value of 6 in 2,465,301 = 60,000. 2) Value of 3 in 7.034 = 0.03 (3 hundredths). 3) 0.9 × 10 = 9. 4) 0.05 × 10 = 0.5. 5) 1/10 of 400 = 40. 6) 1/10 of 0.2 = 0.02. 7) 6 × 100 = 600. 8) In 33.3, the 3 in the ones place is 10 times the 3 in the tenths place. 9) In 444, the first 4 is 100 times the last 4. 10) 0.008 is 1/10 of 0.08. 11) 70 is 10 times 7. 12) Standard form of 5 million 4 thousand 2 hundredths = 5,004,000.02. Written explanation (proficient): each place is worth 10 times the place to its right, so ×10 shifts digits one place left (÷10 one place right) while the decimal point stays fixed between ones and tenths.

weeks.prep: Place value chart, metric ruler or tape measure, calculator for checking only. Choose 5 household objects to measure (book, spoon, pencil, remote, cup).
misconceptions: Counting zeros in the power of 10 but 'adding zeros' to decimals (3.42 × 100 = 3.4200). Use the chart: digits shift left two places, giving 342.
Reading 10^3 as 10 × 3 = 30. Have the child write 10^3 = 10 × 10 × 10 = 1,000.
Forgetting placeholder zeros when dividing (45 ÷ 1,000 written as 0.45). Shift digits three places right and fill empty places with zeros: 0.045.

days.guide: Write 3.42 on the chart and multiply by 10, 100 and 1,000, moving digits left one, two, three places. The child solves 20 problems and writes the pattern: the number of zeros in the power of 10 tells how many places digits shift left.
Model 45 ÷ 10, ÷ 100, ÷ 1,000 on the chart, shifting digits right and filling empty places with zeros. The child solves 20 problems and explains why placeholder zeros are needed.

questions.a: 0.045 — digits shift three places right; a zero holds the tenths place.

days.guide: Show 10^1 = 10, 10^2 = 100, 10^3 = 1,000, 10^4 = 10,000: the exponent tells how many 10s are multiplied (and how many zeros). Do 6 × 10^3 = 6,000 together, then the child solves 15 mixed problems.
Measure 5 objects in centimeters and record in a table. Convert to millimeters (× 10) and meters (÷ 100). Check each conversion makes sense (meters should be the smallest number).

questions.q: A pencil is 18 cm long. How long is it in mm and in m?
questions.a: 180 mm and 0.18 m.

questions.q: Why do you divide by 100 to go from cm to m?
questions.a: There are 100 centimeters in a meter, so a centimeter is 1/100 of a meter.

days.guide: Give the 15-problem quiz; the child then fixes each error on the place value chart and says what went wrong. Score it with the assessment key, then have your child rework each missed problem aloud, naming the error, before you move on.

misconceptions: Thinking 0.35 < 0.305 because 305 > 35. Line up digits by place value or annex zeros: 0.350 vs 0.305.
Using 'and' for whole numbers (three hundred and five). 'And' only marks the decimal point.

days.guide: Model 3.052 in all three forms: standard, word ('three and fifty-two thousandths') and expanded (3 × 1 + 5 × (1/100) + 2 × (1/1,000)). The child converts 12 decimals, checking that 'and' appears only at the decimal point.

questions.q: Write 3.052 in word form and expanded form.

questions.a: Yes. 4 tenths = 40 hundredths = 400 thousandths; the shaded area is identical.

questions.a: 0.305 < 0.35 (3 tenths each, but 0 hundredths < 5 hundredths).

weeks.assessment_key: Suggested key: 1) 'five and twenty-three thousandths' = 5.023 2) 0.716 in words = seven hundred sixteen thousandths 3) 8.409 expanded = 8 × 1 + 4 × (1/10) + 9 × (1/1,000) 4) 2 × 10 + 3 × (1/100) = 20.03 5) 0.7 > 0.69 6) 1.250 = 1.25 7) 3.08 < 3.8 8) 0.099 < 0.1 9) Order 4.5, 4.05, 4.505, 4.055 → 4.05, 4.055, 4.5, 4.505 10) Order 0.3, 0.033, 0.303 → 0.033, 0.3, 0.303. questions.a: 0.6, because 6 tenths > 5 tenths.

weeks.assessment_key: Unit 1 test key (suggested 15 items): 1) Value of 4 in 3.245 = 0.04 2) 0.8 is 10 times 0.08 3) 1/10 of 6 = 0.6 4) 5.3 × 100 = 530 5) 72 ÷ 1,000 = 0.072 6) 10^4 = 10,000 7) 9 × 10^3 = 9,000 8) 'six and fourteen thousandths' = 6.014 9) 0.42 > 0.402 10) Order 1.1, 1.01, 1.101 → 1.01, 1.1, 1.101 11) Round 3.649 to the tenth = 3.6 12) Round 3.649 to the hundredth = 3.65 13) Round 12.5 to the nearest whole = 13 14) Round 0.996 to the hundredth = 1.00 15) Explain why 2.5 × 10 = 25 (digits shift one place left). Scoring: 14–15 mastery, 11–13 proficient, 8–10 developing, below 8 reteach.

weeks.prep: Grid paper (1 digit per square keeps columns aligned), multiplication fact cards, a timer for the 3-minute fact check.
misconceptions: Forgetting the placeholder zero in the second partial product (multiplying by the tens digit). Say 'I'm multiplying by 30, not 3' and write the zero first.
Adding carried digits before multiplying. Multiply first, then add the regrouped digit.
Misaligned columns. Use grid paper and check against an estimate.

days.guide: Model rounding each factor to one non-zero digit: 389 × 42 ≈ 400 × 40 = 16,000 (4 × 4 = 16, then add three zeros). The child estimates 15 products, then does a 3-minute fact check.
Draw a rectangle split into 200 + 30 + 6 by 30 + 4 and fill the 6 boxes. Add the partial products. The child solves 8 problems.
Solve 236 × 34 with the algorithm next to the area model: 236 × 4 = 944 and 236 × 30 = 7,080 are the two rows. The child does 10 three-by-two problems on grid paper.
Model 2,407 × 56 with an estimate first (2,400 × 60 = 144,000). The child solves 10 larger problems (4-by-2 and 3-by-3) and compares each answer to its estimate.
Give the 10-problem quiz. Then show three worked examples with errors (a missing placeholder zero, a regrouping slip, misaligned columns); the child finds and fixes each.

questions.q: A student wrote 53 × 27 = 477. Find the error.
questions.a: They multiplied 53 × 2 = 106 without the placeholder zero and added 371 + 106 = 477. Correct: 371 + 1,060 = 1,431.

weeks.prep: Make expression cards (e.g., (6 + 4) × 3, 6 + 4 × 3, 2 × {5 + [12 − (3 × 2)]}) and gather 4 dice for 'Target 24'. Review order of operations.
misconceptions: Working left to right and ignoring grouping symbols. Highlight the innermost group and do it first.
Writing 'add 8 and 7, then multiply by 2' as 8 + 7 × 2. Parentheses are needed: (8 + 7) × 2.
Thinking you must calculate to compare expressions. Point out the shared part (18,932 + 921) and what is done to it.

days.guide: Evaluate (6 + 4) × 3 and 6 + 4 × 3 side by side and discuss why one is 30 and one is 18. The child evaluates 15 expressions, circling what to do first.

questions.a: 30 vs 18. Parentheses make you add first; without them you multiply first.

days.guide: Model working inside out: parentheses, then brackets, then braces. The child rewrites each step on a new line for 12 problems.
Translate words to expressions and back, underlining action words (add, then, multiply). The child writes 12 expressions and phrases for given expressions.

questions.q: Write: add 8 and 7, then multiply by 2.
questions.a: (8 + 7) × 2, which equals 30.
Subtract 2 from 9, then multiply by 4.

days.guide: Ask why 3 × (18,932 + 921) is three times as large as 18,932 + 921 without calculating (it is the same sum tripled). Then the child solves 5 multi-step multiplication word problems with labeled answers.

questions.a: It is 5 times as large because the same sum is multiplied by 5.

questions.q: Tickets cost $14. A family buys 3 adult and 4 child tickets at the same price. Write and solve an expression.

days.guide: Play 'Target 24': roll four dice and build an expression with grouping symbols equal to 24. Then give the 12-item quiz.

questions.a: One answer: 6 × 4 × (3 − 2) = 24. Another: (6 + 2) × (4 − 3) × 3 = 24. Accept any correct expression that uses each number once.

weeks.assessment_key: Suggested 12-item key: 1) 4 + 5 × 2 = 14 2) (4 + 5) × 2 = 18 3) 30 − (12 + 6) = 12 4) 48 ÷ (4 × 3) = 4 5) 3 × [10 − (2 + 5)] = 9 6) {20 − [3 × (8 − 5)]} × 2 = 22 7) 'multiply 6 by 5, then add 4' = 6 × 5 + 4 8) 'subtract 3 from 11, then divide by 2' = (11 − 3) ÷ 2 9) phrase for 7 × (2 + 9): add 2 and 9, then multiply by 7 10) (1,284 + 37) × 4 is 4 times 1,284 + 37 11) 2 × (15 + 25) = 80 12) [6 × (4 + 1)] − 10 = 20. Word problems: full credit requires an expression, correct computation and a labeled unit.

weeks.prep: Grid paper, base-ten blocks or quick drawings (squares, sticks, dots). Review multiplication facts for 2-digit multiples (24 × 10, × 5, × 2).
misconceptions: Dropping zeros: 2,400 ÷ 60 = 4. Rewrite as 240 tens ÷ 6 tens = 40, then check 60 × 40 = 2,400.
Remainder larger than the divisor. If the remainder ≥ divisor, the quotient can go up by 1.
Forgetting to add the partial quotients at the end. Circle each one and total them.

days.guide: Use basic facts: 2,400 ÷ 60 is like 24 ÷ 6 = 4, then think 60 × 40 = 2,400. The child solves 15 problems, checking each by multiplying.
Draw a rectangle with height 24 and an unknown width; take off chunks such as 24 × 60 = 1,440, leaving 72 = 24 × 3. Add the widths. The child solves 8 problems this way.
List friendly multiples of the divisor (10×, 5×, 2×) at the side, then subtract chunks. The child solves 8 four-digit by two-digit problems.
Solve each problem, then check: quotient × divisor + remainder = dividend. The child writes one sentence on why that proves the answer.

questions.a: Division undoes multiplication: equal groups times the number of groups, plus leftovers, rebuilds the total.

days.guide: Give the quiz of 8 problems; the child shows an area model or partial quotients for every one. Score it with the assessment key, then have your child rework each missed problem aloud, naming the error, before you move on.

weeks.assessment_key: Suggested key: 1) 3,600 ÷ 90 = 40 2) 1,488 ÷ 31 = 48 3) 2,856 ÷ 42 = 68 4) 4,368 ÷ 52 = 84 5) 945 ÷ 15 = 63 6) 2,047 ÷ 23 = 89 7) 5,000 ÷ 25 = 200 8) 1,000 ÷ 37 = 27 R1. Full credit needs a correct answer and a model or partial quotients that matches it.

weeks.prep: Word problem cards (write 8 problems such as 230 students on buses holding 48; 150 pencils in packs of 24). Prepare the Unit 2 test from the key.
misconceptions: Always rounding remainders down. Ask 'what does the leftover mean?' — extra students still need a bus (round up).
Picking non-compatible estimates (3,476 ÷ 58 ≈ 3,500 ÷ 60). Choose numbers that divide easily: 3,600 ÷ 60.
Not adjusting a trial quotient that's too big. If the product is larger than the part being divided, lower the digit by one.

days.guide: Model compatible numbers: 3,476 ÷ 58 ≈ 3,600 ÷ 60 = 60. Since 3,476 < 3,600, the real quotient is a bit less. The child estimates 15 quotients and predicts greater/less.

questions.q: Estimate 3,476 ÷ 58. Is the real answer greater or less?
questions.a: ≈ 3,600 ÷ 60 = 60; the real quotient is less (59 R54).

days.guide: Model a trial quotient that is too high: 245 ÷ 35, try 8 → 280 is too big, try 7 → 245. The child solves 8 problems, showing crossed-out trials.

questions.a: 7 (8 × 35 = 280 is too high).

days.guide: Read each problem and ask what the remainder means. Decide: round up, drop it, or use it as the answer. The child solves 8 word problems and writes the decision.

questions.q: 230 students ride buses holding 48 each. How many buses?
questions.a: 230 ÷ 48 = 4 R38, so 5 buses (round up).

questions.q: 150 pencils are packed 24 to a box. How many full boxes?
questions.a: 6 R6, so 6 full boxes (drop the remainder).

questions.q: How many pencils are left over?
questions.a: 6 (use the remainder).

days.guide: Mixed review of multiplication, expressions and division. For each problem type, the child writes and solves an original word problem.
Give the Unit 2 test independently, then review mistakes together. Score it with the assessment key, then have your child rework each missed problem aloud, naming the error, before you move on.

questions.q: A theater has 1,248 seats in rows of 32. How many rows?

weeks.prep: Hundredths grids, play money, a store flyer or printed online prices. Set a $50 budget for the shopping scenarios.
misconceptions: Lining up the right-most digits (4.7 + 12.35 as 4.7 under 2.35). Line up decimal points and write 4.70.
Subtracting 8 − 2.36 as 2.36 − 8 or getting 6.36. Write 8.00 and regroup.
Forgetting to carry when tenths sum past 10. Use grids: 10 tenths make a whole.

days.guide: Shade 0.46 in one color and 0.38 in another on a hundredths grid, count the total, then write 0.46 + 0.38 = 0.84 with a place value equation. The child models 10 pairs.

questions.a: 0.84 (4 tenths + 3 tenths = 7 tenths; 6 + 8 hundredths = 14 hundredths = 1 tenth 4 hundredths).

days.guide: Line up decimal points, annex zeros so places match, and add with regrouping. The child solves 15 problems.
Model 8 − 2.36 by writing 8.00 and regrouping, then check by adding 5.64 + 2.36 = 8. The child solves 15 problems with an addition check.
Give the child the flyer and $50. For each of 5 scenarios, list items, add prices and subtract from $50 to find the change.

questions.q: You buy items for $12.49, $8.75 and $19.99. How much is left from $50?
questions.a: Total $41.23; change $8.77.

days.guide: Give the 12-problem quiz independently, including 2 word problems; check work by estimating. Score it with the assessment key, then have your child rework each missed problem aloud, naming the error, before you move on.

questions.q: A runner ran 3.75 km then 2.6 km. How far in all?

weeks.prep: Hundredths grids and colored pencils; a price per pound for apples (e.g., $1.29/lb) for the word problems.
misconceptions: Lining up decimal points to multiply. In multiplication, multiply as whole numbers, then place the point.
Believing multiplication always makes bigger. Show 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2 as 'half of 4 tenths.'
Counting decimal places but dropping a needed zero (0.3 × 0.6 = 1.8). The product has 2 decimal places: 0.18.

days.guide: Solve 4 × 0.36 three ways: 0.36 + 0.36 + 0.36 + 0.36, with disks, and 4 × 36 = 144 → 1.44. The child solves 12 problems and compares methods.
Shade 3 columns (0.3) in one color and 6 rows (0.6) in another; the overlap is 18 small squares = 0.18. The child models 8 problems.
Multiply 24 × 13 = 312, then estimate 2.4 × 1.3 ≈ 2 × 1 = 2 or 3 to place the point: 3.12. Confirm by counting two decimal places. The child solves 12 problems both ways.
Solve the apple problem together with an estimate (3.5 × 1.3 ≈ 4.55). The child solves 6 context problems, rounding money to the cent.

questions.q: 3.5 lb of apples at $1.29 per pound costs?

days.guide: Give the 10-problem quiz and have the child explain in writing why 0.5 × 0.4 is smaller than both factors. Score it with the assessment key, then have your child rework each missed problem aloud, naming the error, before you move on.

questions.q: Why is 0.5 × 0.4 = 0.2 smaller than both factors?
questions.a: You are taking half of 0.4 (less than 0.4), and 0.4 of 0.5 (less than 0.5). Multiplying by a number less than 1 makes the product smaller.

weeks.assessment_key: Suggested key: 1) 3 × 0.8 = 2.4 2) 7 × 0.25 = 1.75 3) 0.4 × 0.7 = 0.28 4) 0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81 5) 1.5 × 2.2 = 3.3 6) 3.6 × 0.5 = 1.8 7) 4.25 × 6 = 25.5 8) 0.2 × 0.05 = 0.01 9) 12.3 × 1.1 = 13.53 10) 2.75 × 4 = 11. Explanation (proficient): states that multiplying by a factor less than 1 takes a part of the other number, so the product is smaller than each factor.

weeks.prep: Place value disks (ones, tenths, hundredths) and hundredths grids. Practice 7.5 ÷ 6 yourself so you can model annexing zeros.
misconceptions: Misplacing the decimal point in the quotient. Write the point in the quotient directly above the dividend's point before dividing.
Stopping with a remainder. Annex zeros (7.5 = 7.50) and keep dividing.
Thinking dividing always gives a smaller answer. 2 ÷ 0.5 = 4: there are 4 halves in 2.

days.guide: Share 4.8 (4 ones and 8 tenths disks) among 4 groups: 1 one and 2 tenths each = 1.2. Then show the written method for 6.24 ÷ 3. The child solves 12 problems.
Divide 7.5 ÷ 6: 6 goes into 7 once (1 left), 15 tenths ÷ 6 = 2 R3, annex a zero: 30 hundredths ÷ 6 = 5. The child solves 10 such problems.
Ask 'how many halves in 2?' and shade it: 4. Then 3.6 ÷ 0.4 as 'how many 4 tenths in 36 tenths' = 9. The child solves 10 problems with grids.
Show that multiplying dividend and divisor by the same power of 10 keeps the quotient: 1.44 ÷ 0.12 = 144 ÷ 12 = 12. The child rewrites and solves 10 problems.

Give the 10-problem quiz; the child checks two answers by multiplying quotient × divisor. Score it with the assessment key, then have your child rework each missed problem aloud, naming the error, before you move on.

weeks.prep: A recipe card with decimal amounts (e.g., 1.5 cups flour, 0.75 cup sugar, 2.25 tsp baking powder) and grocery ads or prices with sizes. Write the Unit 3 test.
misconceptions: Choosing operations by key words alone ('each' always means multiply). Draw a bar model to see whether you are combining, comparing, grouping or sharing.
Comparing total prices instead of unit prices. Divide price by size to compare cost per ounce.
Rounding money in the middle of a problem. Keep all digits until the final answer.

days.guide: Read each problem and sketch a bar model before choosing an operation. The child sorts 12 problems into +, −, ×, ÷ and solves 6.

questions.q: A 2.4 m ribbon is cut into 6 equal pieces. How long is each? Which operation?
questions.a: Division: 2.4 ÷ 6 = 0.4 m.

days.guide: Divide price by ounces for each item. The child compares 4 pairs and states the better buy.

questions.q: 12 oz for $3.48 or 16 oz for $4.32 — which is the better buy?
questions.a: $3.48 ÷ 12 = $0.29/oz; $4.32 ÷ 16 = $0.27/oz. The 16 oz is cheaper per ounce.

days.guide: Multiply each recipe amount by 2.5 and divide each by 2, recording two new recipes. Ask your child to estimate first (2.5 times is between 2 and 3 times as much). Have them write the scaled recipes in a table: original, × 2.5, ÷ 2.

questions.a: 3.75 cups; 0.75 cup.
1.875 cups

days.guide: Do a mixed review of all four decimal operations, then the child starts a 'my mistakes' log listing errors and the fix for each. Pull problems your child missed on earlier quizzes. For each log entry they write the wrong step, the correct step and a tip to remember.

Give the Unit 3 test independently and review errors against the mistakes log. Score it with the assessment key, then have your child rework each missed problem aloud, naming the error, before you move on.

questions.q: Pencils cost $0.35 each. How many can you buy with $5?

weeks.prep: Fraction strips (or paper strips folded into halves, fourths, eighths, thirds, sixths), and a set of fraction cards for matching (e.g., 6/8 and 3/4).
misconceptions: Adding the same number to top and bottom (1/2 = 2/3). Equivalent fractions multiply or divide both by the same number.
Not simplifying fully (12/18 → 6/9). Use the greatest common factor or keep dividing until no common factor remains.
Thinking bigger denominators mean bigger fractions. Compare 1/3 and 1/8 with strips.

days.guide: Fold a strip in half, then fourths, then eighths to show 1/2 = 2/4 = 4/8. The child generates 3 equivalent fractions for each of 10 fractions by multiplying top and bottom by the same number.
Find common factors of numerator and denominator and divide. The child simplifies 15 fractions, then matches cards.

questions.a: 2/3 (divide by 6).

days.guide: List multiples of each denominator to find the least common multiple; rename both fractions. The child does 12 pairs.

questions.q: Rename 2/3 and 3/4 with a common denominator.

days.guide: Compare 3/5 and 4/7 by renaming (21/35 vs 20/35). Also compare by benchmarks: 5/8 > 1/2 > 3/7. The child compares 12 pairs.

questions.a: 5/8 is more than 1/2 and 3/7 is less than 1/2, so 5/8 > 3/7.

days.guide: Give the quiz independently; correct with strips. Score it with the assessment key, then have your child rework each missed problem aloud, naming the error, before you move on.

questions.a: Yes, divide both by 3.

weeks.assessment_key: Suggested key: 1) 3/4 = 9/12 2) 2/5 = 8/20 3) simplify 8/12 = 2/3 4) simplify 10/25 = 2/5 5) simplify 18/24 = 3/4 6) common denominator for 1/6 and 3/8 = 24: 4/24 and 9/24 7) 2/3 and 1/5 → 10/15 and 3/15 8) 3/4 > 5/8 9) 2/3 < 7/9 10) 4/9 < 1/2 < 5/9. Full credit: correct equivalent forms shown.

weeks.prep: Fraction strips; optional free Math Learning Center Fractions app. Review finding common denominators.
misconceptions: Adding numerators and denominators (1/2 + 1/3 = 2/5). Show with strips that 2/5 is less than 1/2 — impossible for a sum.
Renaming only one fraction. Both fractions must have the common denominator.
Leaving improper answers or unsimplified answers. Convert to a mixed number and simplify.

days.guide: Lay a 1/2 and a 1/3 strip end to end and find which single strip size fits exactly: sixths, 5/6. Record 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6. The child models 8 more pairs.
Rename both fractions with a common denominator, add numerators, then convert sums > 1 to mixed numbers. The child solves 15.
Draw a number line in twelfths; mark 3/4 (9/12) and jump back 1/6 (2/12) to land on 7/12. The child models 8 more.
Rename, subtract numerators, simplify. The child solves 15 problems.

Give the 12-problem quiz independently and check answers with benchmark estimates. Score it with the assessment key, then have your child rework each missed problem aloud, naming the error, before you move on.

weeks.prep: Fraction circles, measuring cups (1/2, 1/3, 2/3, 1 cup) and a clear container that holds at least 3 cups of water.
misconceptions: Subtracting the smaller fraction from the larger regardless of order (5 1/4 − 2 2/3 = 3 5/12). Rename first: 3/12 − 8/12 needs regrouping.
Regrouping a whole as 10 (like base ten). One whole = 12/12, 4/4, etc., matching the denominator.
Leaving 3 17/12 as a final answer. Rename 17/12 as 1 5/12 and add the whole: 4 5/12.

days.guide: Show 2 3/4 with fraction circles and count the fourths: 11/4. Then the shortcut: 2 × 4 + 3 = 11. Reverse: 17/5 → 3 wholes and 2/5. The child converts 15 numbers.
Add wholes and fractions separately after renaming: 2 9/12 + 1 8/12 = 3 17/12 = 4 5/12. The child solves 12.
Rename, check if the fraction part can be subtracted, and if not, regroup one whole: 5 3/12 → 4 15/12. The child solves 12.
Pour 1 1/2 cups and 2/3 cup of water into the container. Compute the total, then how much more makes 3 cups; check by pouring.

questions.q: 1 1/2 + 2/3 cups = ? How much more to make 3 cups?
questions.a: 2 1/6 cups; 5/6 cup more.

days.guide: Give the quiz independently; check with estimation (each answer should be near the whole-number estimate). Score it with the assessment key, then have your child rework each missed problem aloud, naming the error, before you move on.

weeks.prep: Number lines labeled 0, 1/2, 1, 1 1/2, 2…; word problem cards. Write out the 8 'reasonable?' solutions for Day 3.
misconceptions: Rounding every fraction to 1. Use the 0, 1/2, 1 benchmarks: is the numerator about half the denominator, near zero, or near the denominator?
Accepting answers without checking. Always compare the exact answer to the estimate.
Using the wrong operation for 'how much farther' (adds instead of subtracting). Draw a comparison bar model.

days.guide: Model: 7/8 is close to 1, 4/9 is close to 1/2, so 7/8 + 4/9 ≈ 1 1/2. The child estimates 15 sums and differences on number lines.

questions.a: About 1 − 0 = 1.

days.guide: Draw a bar for 2 1/3 and another for 1 3/4 joined, then solve with an equation. The child solves 6 problems with bar models and labeled answers.

questions.q: A hiker walked 2 1/3 miles then 1 3/4 miles. How far in all?

days.guide: Present each worked solution; the child compares it to a benchmark estimate, labels reasonable/not, and fixes wrong ones. Model one: 2/5 + 1/2 must be more than 1/2, so 3/7 can't be right. Your child writes the benchmark reasoning for each of the 8.

questions.a: No. 3/7 is less than 1/2, but the sum must be more than 1/2. Correct: 4/10 + 5/10 = 9/10.

days.guide: The child writes and solves 4 garden or recipe word problems, including one subtraction requiring regrouping. Check each solution together.

questions.q: Write and solve a regrouping subtraction: a 4 1/4 ft board, cut off 1 3/4 ft.

days.guide: Give the word-problem quiz; each answer needs a model, equation, answer and estimate check. Score it with the assessment key, then have your child rework each missed problem aloud, naming the error, before you move on.

questions.q: Jo had 3 1/2 cups of flour and used 1 2/3. How much is left?
questions.a: 1 5/6 cups (estimate 3 1/2 − 1 1/2 = 2).

weeks.assessment_key: Rubric per problem (4 pts): model (bar/number line) 1, equation 1, correct labeled answer 1, estimate check 1. Suggested problems and answers: 1) 1 1/2 + 2 2/3 = 4 1/6 2) 5 − 2 3/8 = 2 5/8 3) 3/4 + 5/6 = 1 7/12 4) 4 1/3 − 2 1/2 = 1 5/6. 14–16 proficient/mastery, 10–13 developing.

weeks.prep: Ruler marked in eighths of an inch, 12 pencils or leaves, measuring cups. Practice reading eighths on the ruler.
misconceptions: Reading the ruler from 1 instead of 0. Line the object up at 0.
Spacing a line plot unevenly. Mark every 1/8 at equal intervals even if no data falls there.
Adding line plot values by counting Xs instead of their values. Multiply each value by its number of Xs, then add.

days.guide: Show how to read eighths on the ruler (1/4 = 2/8, 1/2 = 4/8). The child measures 12 items to the nearest 1/8 inch and records them in a table.

questions.q: A pencil ends 3 marks past the 5. Each mark is 1/8. How long is it?
questions.a: 5 3/8 inches.

days.guide: Draw a number line covering the data's range in eighths, add an X per measurement, a title and units. Check that marks are evenly spaced.

questions.q: Why include 5 1/8 on the line if no item measured that?
questions.a: The scale must have equal intervals; empty values show there is no data there.

days.guide: Use the plot to find total length and the difference between longest and shortest. Then solve the beaker problem: redistribute liquid equally.

questions.q: Beakers hold 1/4, 1/2, 1/2 and 3/4 L. If shared equally, how much in each?
questions.a: Total 2 L ÷ 4 = 1/2 L each.
2 1/2 inches.
